[[File:Nertera granadensis on Cerro de la Muerte.JPG|thumb|''Nertera granadensis'' in fruit on Cerro de la Muerte, Costa Rica]]
'''''Nertera granadensis''''', also known as '''coral bead plant''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = January 21, 2018}}</ref> '''pin-cushion plant''',{{citation needed|date=August 2013}} '''coral moss''',<ref name=GRIN/> or '''English baby tears''',<ref name=GRIN/> is a plant in the family Rubiaceae with orange berries, of the genus ''[[Nertera]]''.  ''Nertera granadensis'' with an unusually extensive transcontinental distribution surrounding the [[Pacific Ocean]], occurring from southern [[Chile]] and western [[Argentina]] north to [[Guatemala]], and in [[Hawaii]], [[New Zealand]], eastern [[Australia]], [[Indonesia]], [[Malaysia]], [[Papua New Guinea]], the [[Philippines]] and [[Taiwan]], possibly due to its cultivation as ground-cover.<ref name="Nertera granadensis">{{cite web|url=http://www.plantfacts.com/Family/Rubiaceae/Nertera.granadensis.shtml|title=Nertera granadensis|year=2008|accessdate=2008-01-25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://botany.si.edu/pacificislandbiodiversity/hawaiianflora/speciesdescr.cfm?genus=Nertera&species=granadensis|title=Flora of the Hawaiian Islands}}</ref> In tropical biomes of the western Pacific,  ''Nertera granadensis'' only occurs at high altitudes. It does also occur on the [[Juan Fernández Islands]].<ref name=Chileflora/> It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens, and the name given to the plant in [[Mapudungun]] and [[Chilean Spanish]] is ''rucachucao''.<ref name=Chileflora>[http://www.florachilena.cl/Niv_tax/Angiospermas/Ordenes/Gentianales/Rubiaceae/Nertera/Nertera%20granadensis/Nertera%20granadensis.htm Flora chilena]</ref> The name ''granadensis'' derives from New Granada, the old name of [[Colombia]].<ref name=Chileflora/>

==Care and maintenance==
As a houseplant, ''Nertera granadensis'' is somewhat difficult to maintain, and it is not recommended for beginners. The soil should provide adequate drainage. It should be kept in a bright, semi-shaded place - a tropic-facing window is ideal - and should not be left in direct sunlight.<ref name="weekendgardener.net">{{cite web|url=http://www.weekendgardener.net/2006/06/nertera-granadensis-caring-for-house.htm|title=Nertera granadensis - caring for house plants|date=2006-06-20|accessdate=2008-01-25}}</ref>

During the summer, ''Nertera granadensis'' can be kept outdoors, but it still needs to be protected from direct sunlight. Its environment should not be too warm, nor should it go below 8 degrees Celsius (around 45 Fahrenheit) in the winter for the plant to thrive.<ref name="weekendgardener.net"/>  During the winter and autumn gardeners should wait until the soil dries between watering.<ref name="weekendgardener.net"/>

When flowers and berries begin forming in the spring, one should increase watering so that during spring and summer the soil is kept moist at all times. The leaves and berries should be moistened occasionally, but not too frequently, as they could rot.<ref name="Nertera granadensis"/> The plant should be fed monthly with a weak solution (water-soluble fertilizers, diluted to half strength, are best) during spring/summer until it begins to flower.<ref>Citation needed.</ref> When the berries turn black they should be carefully removed.<ref>Citation needed.</ref>

==Toxicity==
The plant possesses brightly colored fruit, and can be visually appealing to young children and pets.  A publication by some German scientists noted that of 21 children known to have ingested the plant, five showed mild symptoms associated with poisoning, such as tiredness, stomach pains, and vomiting.<ref name="Frohne, Dietrich and Pfänder, Hans Jürgen 2005 344">{{cite book|title=Poisonous Plants: A Handbook for Doctors, Pharmacists, Toxicologists|author1=Frohne, Dietrich  |author2=Pfänder, Hans Jürgen |name-list-style=amp |year=2005|page=344}}</ref>
